name: Giant cell (temporal) arteritis

matching.reasoningTemplate: New headache with visual symptoms in a patient over 50 with raised inflammatory markers suggests giant cell arteritis.

redFlags: Visual loss is an emergency — do not delay steroids

harrison.pages: Harrison 22e p.115 (Ch.17 Headache), p.227 (Ch.34 Disorders of the Eye / AION), p.2902-2903 (Ch.375 Vasculitis Syndromes)
clinicalPearls: Occurs almost exclusively in people over 50; mean age of onset around 70, with women making up roughly two-thirds of cases. Rare in Black patients; higher incidence in Scandinavian populations (Harrison 22e p.115, p.2902).
Four phenotypic patterns can occur together, in isolation, or at different times: cranial arteritis, polymyalgia rheumatica, large-vessel disease, and systemic inflammation (Harrison 22e p.2902).

Headache is the dominant cranial symptom; it is usually dull/boring rather than throbbing, may be unilateral or bilateral, is temporally located in only about half of patients, often worse at night, and aggravated by cold (Harrison 22e p.115).

Scalp tenderness can be marked - brushing hair or resting the head on a pillow may be intolerable; the temporal (or less often occipital) artery may be tender, thickened, nodular, reddened or have overlying red skin streaks (Harrison 22e p.115).
The temporal artery may pulsate early in disease but can become occluded later (Harrison 22e p.2902).
Jaw and tongue claudication and scalp pain are recognized cranial-ischemic features; rarer cranial ischemic events include stroke and scalp or tongue infarction (Harrison 22e p.115, p.2902).
ESR and/or CRP are elevated in most patients, but a normal ESR does NOT exclude giant cell arteritis (Harrison 22e p.115).
Other supportive labs: normochromic or slightly hypochromic anemia, raised alkaline phosphatase (liver function abnormalities common), and increased IgG and complement (Harrison 22e p.2902).
Most patients report head or eye complaints before any visual loss, so attention to early cranial symptoms with prompt therapy reduces the risk of blindness (Harrison 22e p.2902).

Polymyalgia rheumatica overlaps strongly: PMR is seen in 40-50% of GCA patients, and 10-20% who present with isolated PMR later develop GCA - GCA and PMR are regarded as a spectrum of one disease process (Harrison 22e p.2902).

In PMR, creatine kinase is not elevated and rheumatoid factor / anti-CCP should be negative; a worsening peripheral arthritis pattern should prompt reconsideration of seronegative RA or other inflammatory arthropathy (Harrison 22e p.2903).
harrison.pathophysiology: A panarteritis of medium- and large-sized arteries, classically branches of the carotid (especially the temporal artery) but systemically involving the aorta and its branches. Histology shows mononuclear inflammatory infiltrate within the vessel wall with frequent giant cell formation, intimal proliferation, and fragmentation of the internal elastic lamina; organ damage results from ischemia of involved vessels. It is considered an antigen-driven process: CD4+ T cells enter via the adventitial vasa vasorum, become activated, and drive macrophage differentiation, with restricted clonal T-cell expansion suggesting an arterial-wall antigen. Lesional T cells produce mainly IL-2 and IFN-gamma; both IFN-gamma-producing TH1 and IL-17-producing TH17 lineages contribute and may differ in glucocorticoid responsiveness. Associated with HLA-DR4 and HLA-DRB1*04 variants. (Harrison 22e p.2902)
additionalDifferentials: Migraine - common in the elderly (more prevalent than GCA) and may improve with prednisone, so a steroid response does not by itself confirm GCA (Harrison 22e p.115).

Nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy - associated with a crowded 'disc-at-risk' / small optic cup, in which glucocorticoids should NOT be prescribed, contrasting with the arteritic form (Harrison 22e p.227).
Isolated polymyalgia rheumatica without arteritis (Harrison 22e p.2903).
Other inflammatory causes of secondary headache such as sarcoidosis and Behcet's syndrome (Harrison 22e p.115).
nonInfectiousMimics: Seronegative rheumatoid arthritis or other inflammatory arthropathy mimicking the peripheral arthritis of PMR (Harrison 22e p.2903).
additionalInvestigations: Temporal artery biopsy: yield improved by harvesting a long segment (3-5 cm) with serial sectioning because involvement is segmental/patchy; biopsy may still show vasculitis even after about 14 days of glucocorticoids, but prolonged treatment can mask findings (Harrison 22e p.227, p.2903).
Temporal artery ultrasonography (alone or with axillary arteries) showing a noncompressible 'halo' sign supports the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.2903).

Large-vessel imaging by MR or CT angiography to confirm large-vessel disease suggested by diminished pulses or bruits; PET is increasingly studied but its diagnostic/monitoring role remains unclear (Harrison 22e p.2903).
Note: in patients treated with an IL-6 inhibitor, CRP and ESR normalize and can no longer be used to monitor disease activity or assess for infection (Harrison 22e p.2902).
redFlags: Ischemic optic neuropathy is the dreaded complication; about half of untreated patients develop blindness from ophthalmic-artery involvement, and arteritic AION is the leading cause of rapidly developing bilateral blindness in patients over 60 (Harrison 22e p.115).

In suspected arteritic AION / visual loss, start glucocorticoids IMMEDIATELY without waiting for biopsy to protect vision in the fellow eye - a sight-saving principle; do not delay therapy pending diagnostic studies (Harrison 22e p.227, p.2903).
Sudden visual loss / blindness can be the presenting or emergent feature (Harrison 22e p.2902).
Aortic aneurysm: GCA patients are 18 times more likely than the general population to develop thoracic aortic aneurysms, carrying risk of rupture or dissection (Harrison 22e p.2903).
Subclavian stenosis presenting as arm claudication signals large-vessel involvement (Harrison 22e p.2902).
harrison.prognosis: Acute mortality directly from GCA is uncommon; when fatal it is usually due to cerebrovascular events or myocardial infarction. The main late mortality risk is rupture or dissection of an aortic aneurysm (18-fold increased thoracic aortic aneurysm risk). Disease is highly glucocorticoid-responsive but relapsing: symptom recurrence during steroid tapering occurs in 60-85% of patients, most require at least 2 years of treatment, and glucocorticoid toxicity affects 35-65% and is a major source of morbidity. (Harrison 22e p.2903)
pitfalls: A normal ESR does not rule out GCA (Harrison 22e p.115).
A single negative temporal artery biopsy does not exclude the disease because lesions are segmental/patchy - take a long segment and serial sections (Harrison 22e p.2903).
Improvement of headache on prednisone is non-specific (migraine also responds), so do not use the steroid response alone to confirm GCA (Harrison 22e p.115).
Once an IL-6 inhibitor is started, ESR/CRP can no longer track activity or flag infection (Harrison 22e p.2902).
Minor ESR/CRP rises during tapering may reflect other causes (including infection) rather than a true flare, especially in a symptom-free patient (Harrison 22e p.2903).
Glucocorticoids should not be given for the nonarteritic form of AION - distinguishing arteritic from nonarteritic AION matters (Harrison 22e p.227).
